questions.text: A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s. Taking upward as positive and g = 9.8 m/s², what is its displacement at t = 3 s?
solution_steps: Write s = ut + ½at² with a = −9.8 m/s².

b.explanation: Used +9.8 for gravity in an up-positive frame: s = 20·3 + 0.5·9.8·9 = 104.1 m.
b.student_note: Gravity was counted as +9.8 while up was positive. Try this bridge: keep the − sign on every gravity term.

c.explanation: Computed s = u·t only, omitting ½at².
c.student_note: The acceleration term went missing. Next bridge: write the full equation first, then substitute.

d.explanation: Squared time as 6 instead of 9: 60 − 0.5·9.8·6 = 30.6 m.
d.student_note: One computation slipped (3² = 9). A quick estimate-first habit bridges this.

questions.text: A particle moves with position x(t) = 3t³ (metres, seconds). Find its velocity at t = 2 s.
solution_steps: Constant-acceleration formulas need constant a — here a changes.
Differentiate: v = dx/dt = 9t², so v(2) = 36 m/s.

options.text: Cannot be determined — a is not given

b.explanation: Reached for v = u + at (needs constant a) on x(t) = 3t³.
b.student_note: v = u + at only fits constant acceleration. Bridge: differentiate x(t) when a varies.

c.explanation: Reported position x(2) = 24 m as velocity.
c.student_note: 24 m is the position at t = 2. The bridge: velocity is the rate of change of position.

d.student_note: The derivative setup was right; one computation slipped.

questions.text: A stone is dropped from a 45 m cliff. How long to reach the ground? (g = 9.8 m/s²)

options.text: Cannot be determined — u and v are missing

b.student_note: The word 'dropped' already gives u = 0. Bridge: list what the words imply before solving.

c.explanation: Divided 45/9.8 = 4.59 s, ignoring the ½t² structure.
c.student_note: Free fall is accelerated, not uniform. Bridge: start from s = ut + ½at².

d.explanation: Computed 2·45/9.8 = 9.18 but skipped the square root.
d.student_note: Setup was right; the final square root slipped past.

questions.text: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. What distance does it cover?

b.student_note: Only the final speed was used. Bridge: average velocity × time, or the full equation.

c.explanation: Used s = u·t = 50 m, omitting ½at².
c.student_note: The acceleration term went missing — write the full equation first.

d.explanation: Right setup, arithmetic landing on 80 m.
d.student_note: Setup was right; one computation slipped.

questions.text: A projectile is launched at 30 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. What is its initial vertical velocity?

b.student_note: Vertical needs sin, horizontal needs cos. Bridge: label the triangle first.

c.student_note: 30 m/s is the full speed, not its vertical part.

d.explanation: Component setup right, arithmetic landing on 17.3.
d.student_note: Setup was right; one computation slipped.

questions.text: A car at 20 m/s brakes uniformly at 5 m/s² to rest. Stopping distance?

b.explanation: Dropped the 2 in v² = u² + 2as: 400/5 = 80 m.
b.student_note: The factor 2 went missing. Bridge: write the full equation before substituting.

c.explanation: Setup right, arithmetic landing on 4 m.
c.student_note: Setup was right; one computation slipped.

d.explanation: Mishandled signs in the braking equation, inflating to 100 m.
d.student_note: Braking means a opposes motion — carry the sign through.

questions.text: A sprinter covers 100 m in 9.8 s. Average speed in km/h?

b.student_note: The number was right, the unit step was skipped. Bridge: convert to the asked unit last.

c.student_note: m/s → km/h is ×3.6. One conversion habit to build.

d.student_note: Estimate first (≈36 km/h for a sprinter) to catch slips.

questions.text: A ball is thrown up at 15 m/s. What is its velocity at the peak?
solution_steps: 'At the peak' the ball momentarily stops rising.

b.explanation: Repeated the launch speed at the peak.
b.student_note: 'At the peak' sets v = 0. Bridge: translate the words into values first.

c.explanation: Assumed symmetric return speed at the peak.
c.student_note: −15 m/s happens back at launch height, not at the peak.

d.explanation: Answered with g instead of velocity.
d.student_note: The question asked for velocity — g is acceleration. A 20-second restate helps.

questions.text: A train starts from rest and accelerates at 1.2 m/s² for 20 s. How far does it travel?

b.student_note: Estimate first: 1 m/s² for 20 s is already 200+ m.

c.explanation: Used s = at² = 480 m, dropping ½.
c.student_note: The ½ in ½at² went missing — full equation first.

d.explanation: Answered with a·t/2 = 12 (a speed, not distance).
d.student_note: 12 has speed units. Bridge: check units of the answer.

questions.text: Which list gives only scalar quantities?

b.explanation: Listed displacement and velocity as scalars.
b.student_note: Displacement and velocity carry direction. Bridge: ask 'does direction matter?' per quantity.

c.explanation: Listed velocity and acceleration as scalars.
c.student_note: Velocity and acceleration are vectors.

d.explanation: Listed displacement and force as scalars.

questions.text: Up is positive. A stone falls downward. What is the sign of its velocity?

b.explanation: Took downward motion as positive in an up-positive frame.
b.student_note: Down is negative when up is positive.

c.student_note: Falling means moving — velocity is not zero.

d.explanation: Claimed indeterminable; frame is fully given.
d.student_note: The frame is fully given — commit to the sign.

questions.text: Up is positive, g = 9.8 m/s². What is 'a' for a freely falling body?

b.explanation: Assigned +9.8 to gravity in an up-positive frame.
b.student_note: Gravity points down, so it is −9.8 here.

c.student_note: Free fall still accelerates — only the velocity can be zero.

d.student_note: g is constant near Earth, independent of speed.

questions.text: Up is positive. A ball tossed up at 12 m/s: which expression gives s at t = 2 s?

b.student_note: Keep the minus on gravity throughout.

c.student_note: The ½at² term went missing.

d.student_note: Both terms count — ut carries the launch.

questions.text: A coin is 'released from rest' from a tower. What is u?

b.student_note: 9.8 is the acceleration, not the starting speed.

c.student_note: 'From rest' is the value: u = 0.

d.student_note: Starting speed does not depend on height.

questions.text: a(t) = 6t. Can v = u + at be used directly?
solution_steps: v = u + at assumes constant a.
Here a varies, so integrate: v = u + 3t².

b.explanation: Substituted varying a into a constant-a formula.
b.student_note: That formula needs constant a — integrate instead.

c.explanation: Averaged a to force-fit the formula.
c.student_note: Averaging hides how a changes.

questions.text: A ball is launched at 20 m/s at 60° above horizontal. Initial vertical component? (sin60° ≈ 0.866)

b.student_note: Vertical needs sin: 20·0.866.

c.student_note: 20 m/s is the full speed, not its vertical part.

questions.text: A block rests on a table. Which forces act on the block?

b.student_note: The table pushes back up. Bridge: list every contact.

c.student_note: Weight acts even at rest.

d.explanation: Added friction with no horizontal push.
d.student_note: No horizontal push means no friction here.

questions.text: A 4 kg block is pushed by a net 12 N force. Its acceleration?

b.student_note: Force is divided by mass, not multiplied. Bridge: a = F/m.

c.student_note: Check: bigger force means bigger a — 0.33 is off.

d.student_note: Force and mass combine by division here, not addition.

questions.text: μs = 0.4 for a 10 kg block (g = 10). Maximum static friction?

b.student_note: Normal = mg = 100 N first, then × μ.

c.student_note: 100 N is the normal force; friction is μ times that.

d.student_note: μ has no units of force — multiply by N.

questions.text: Two masses 3 kg and 2 kg hang over a pulley. Acceleration of the system? (g = 10)
solution_steps: Net pull = (3−2)·10 = 10 N; total mass 5 kg.

b.explanation: Used g directly as the system acceleration.
b.student_note: Both masses share one acceleration — divide net pull by total mass.

c.student_note: Total moving mass is 3 + 2 = 5 kg.

d.student_note: 3 kg outweighs 2 kg, so the system moves.

questions.text: A 2 kg object moves at constant velocity. Net force on it?

b.student_note: Steady motion needs zero net force, not zero speed.

c.student_note: Weight acts, but net force is still zero at constant velocity.

d.student_note: Net force depends on acceleration, which is zero here.

questions.text: A block is pushed right on rough ground and moves at steady speed. Friction points?
solution_steps: Motion is right, so friction points left.

b.student_note: Friction opposes the sliding, so it points left here.

c.student_note: The sliding is horizontal — friction is horizontal too.

d.explanation: Set friction zero at steady speed.
d.student_note: Steady speed means friction balances the push, not zero.

questions.text: A 5 kg block on a smooth 30° incline. Acceleration down the slope? (g = 10)

b.explanation: Used full g along the slope.
b.student_note: Only the along-slope component pulls: g·sin30°.

c.student_note: Along the slope is sin; cos is into the slope.

questions.text: A book is pressed against a vertical wall and does not slide. Friction acts?
solution_steps: Weight pulls down; static friction balances it.

b.student_note: Friction fights the slide — the book would slide down, so friction is up.

c.student_note: Into the wall is the normal force, not friction.

d.student_note: At rest, friction is exactly what holds the book up.

questions.text: In a tug-of-war both teams pull 500 N and nobody moves. Tension in the rope?

b.student_note: Tension is one pull, not the sum. Bridge: cut the rope mentally and balance one side.

c.student_note: No motion means balanced — the rope is still taut at 500 N.

d.student_note: No halving here — each side feels the full 500 N.

questions.text: A lift accelerates upward. Your apparent weight?
solution_steps: Upward acceleration needs extra normal force.

b.student_note: Upward acceleration pushes the floor harder into you.

c.student_note: N = mg only when acceleration is zero.

questions.text: A ball hangs from a string at rest. Which diagram is complete?
solution_steps: List forces: weight down, tension up.

b.student_note: Weight always acts — include it.

c.student_note: The string pulls up — include tension.

d.student_note: Only draw forces that act — no air push here.

questions.text: A 6 kg cart gets a 3 N push along the track and a 4 N push sideways. Net acceleration magnitude?

b.student_note: Perpendicular pushes combine as vectors (5 N), then divide by mass.

c.student_note: Combine as vectors first: 5 N, then 5/6.

questions.text: μk = 0.2, N = 50 N. Kinetic friction?

b.student_note: μ is a ratio — multiply by N.

c.student_note: N is the normal; friction is μ·N.

d.student_note: Friction here is just μ·N = 10 N.

questions.text: Two blocks (2 kg + 3 kg) are pushed together by 10 N on smooth ground. Acceleration of the pair?

b.student_note: They move as one — total mass 5 kg.

c.student_note: Total mass is 2 + 3 = 5 kg.

d.student_note: 10 N is the push; acceleration is F/m.

questions.text: A 10 N force acts at 60° above horizontal. Horizontal component?

b.student_note: Horizontal is cos; vertical is sin.

c.student_note: Only the along-axis part counts: 5 N.

questions.text: m = 2 kg, a = 4 m/s². Net force?

b.student_note: Multiply: 2·4 = 8 N.

c.student_note: F = ma is multiplication.

questions.text: A 10 N force pushes a box 4 m in the direction of the force. Work done?

b.student_note: Work multiplies force by distance: 40 J.

c.student_note: Multiply here, not divide.

d.student_note: 10·4 = 40. Estimate first to catch extra zeros.

questions.text: A porter carries luggage horizontally at steady speed. Work done by the carrying (vertical) force?
solution_steps: Force is vertical, displacement horizontal: θ = 90°.

b.explanation: Ignored the angle between force and displacement.
b.student_note: Perpendicular force and motion give zero work — check the angle.

c.explanation: Assigned negative for any vertical force.
c.student_note: Sign comes from cosθ; at 90° it is exactly zero.

questions.text: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s is stopped by friction. Work done by friction?

b.explanation: Dropped the minus: friction removes energy.
b.student_note: Friction opposes motion, so its work is negative.

c.student_note: Zero final KE still means −36 J was removed.

questions.text: A block slides down a rough incline and slows. Can mgh_top = ½mv²_bottom be used directly?
solution_steps: Friction does negative work, so include it.

b.student_note: Friction present means account for its work first.

c.student_note: Friction removes mechanical energy here.

d.student_note: Energy converts to heat — track where it goes.

questions.text: A 1 kg ball drops 5 m (g = 10, no air). Speed at ground?

b.student_note: Energy equates to ½mv² — the square root matters.

c.student_note: √100 = 10. Check the root.

questions.text: An engine does 6000 J in 30 s. Power?

b.student_note: Power divides work by time.

c.student_note: Power is a rate — divide.

questions.text: A 0.5 kg ball at 8 m/s doubles its speed. Net work done on it?

b.student_note: Square first, then subtract: v² − u².

c.explanation: Used m(v²−u²) without ½: 96? no — 24 suggests half of 48 via u² only.
c.student_note: Both speeds count: ½m(v² − u²).

questions.text: Force 5 N pulls at 60° to the direction of motion over 10 m. Work?

b.student_note: The angle term cos60° = 0.5 still multiplies.

c.student_note: Work uses cos of the angle with motion.

d.student_note: cos60° is positive — work is +25 J.

questions.text: A motor lifts 100 N at 2 m/s. Power delivered?

b.student_note: Power multiplies force by velocity.

c.student_note: P = F·v is multiplication.

questions.text: Which situation conserves mechanical energy?

b.student_note: Brakes convert motion to heat — not conserved.

c.student_note: Rough floor drains mechanical energy.

d.student_note: A thud means energy left as sound/heat.

questions.text: A 8 N push moves a crate 5 m along the push. Work?

b.student_note: Work multiplies: 8·5.

c.student_note: Multiply force by distance.

questions.text: A 4 kg cart at 3 m/s is pushed until it reaches 5 m/s. Net work?

b.student_note: Square each speed first, then subtract.

c.student_note: Subtract the starting KE too.

d.student_note: 18 J is where it started — work is the change: 32 J.

questions.text: A pendulum swings in vacuum with no friction at the pivot. Mechanical energy?

b.student_note: Motion converts energy; nothing adds it here.

c.student_note: Nothing drains it here — no friction, no air.

questions.text: A 3 kg block slides down a smooth 4 m-high ramp (g = 10). Speed at bottom?

b.student_note: Energy equates to ½mv² — the root matters.

c.student_note: 4 m is the drop, not the speed.

questions.text: Which unit equals one joule?

b.student_note: Per second is a rate — joule is force times distance.

c.student_note: kg·m/s is momentum, not energy.

d.student_note: W·s is a joule; extra s breaks it.

questions.text: A 2 kg block glides on smooth ice at steady 3 m/s. Mechanical energy?

b.student_note: Motion converts energy; smooth ice adds none.

c.student_note: Nothing drains it on smooth ice.

questions.text: A 6 V battery drives 2 A through a resistor. Resistance?

b.student_note: Resistance divides voltage by current.

c.student_note: V over I: 6/2 = 3.

questions.text: Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel. Equivalent resistance?

b.student_note: Parallel combines by reciprocals — check which rules apply.

c.student_note: Two paths conduct better than one: less than 6 Ω.

questions.text: Two 4 Ω resistors in series. Equivalent resistance?

b.student_note: Series is the simple sum — save reciprocals for parallel.

c.student_note: Two resistors both count.

questions.text: A 2 A current flows through 5 Ω. Heating power?

b.student_note: I·R is voltage; power squares the current: I²R.

c.student_note: Resistance is not squared — current is.

questions.text: Going clockwise round a loop, you pass a battery from − to +. The potential change is?

b.student_note: − to + gains potential. Bridge: mark +/− at each crossing.

c.explanation: Claimed no change crossing a battery.
c.student_note: Crossing a battery always changes potential.

questions.text: An ammeter reads 250 mA through 10 Ω. Voltage across it?

b.student_note: mA → A first: 250 mA = 0.25 A.

c.student_note: Three zeros in milli: 0.25 A, so 2.5 V.

d.student_note: Multiply by 10 Ω to get voltage.

questions.text: A 12 V battery across a parallel pair (4 Ω, 4 Ω). Total current?

b.explanation: Treated as series: 12/8 then halved? 3 A.
b.student_note: Parallel halves resistance first: R = 2 Ω.

c.student_note: 8 Ω is the series value — this pair is parallel.

questions.text: A bulb draws 0.5 A at 220 V. Power?

b.student_note: Power multiplies V by I.

c.student_note: P = VI is multiplication.

questions.text: An ideal voltmeter is connected across a resistor. It draws?

b.student_note: 'Ideal' voltmeter draws (almost) nothing — that is the point.

c.student_note: Nothing doubles here — reread the meter type.

d.student_note: Ammeters go in series; voltmeters sit across.

questions.text: Three identical bulbs in series; one fuses (opens). The others?
solution_steps: Open loop means all go off.

b.student_note: That happens in parallel. Series is one loop — open means dark.

c.student_note: Independence is a parallel trait.

d.student_note: No current at all flows — fully off.

questions.text: Two 10 Ω resistors in series, then that pair in parallel with another 10 Ω. R_eq?
solution_steps: Series pair = 20 Ω; parallel with 10 Ω.

b.student_note: Combine stage by stage: series first, then parallel.

c.student_note: All three resistors count.

d.student_note: Two are in series with each other first.

questions.text: Loop: +12 V battery, then drops of 4 V and 5 V across two resistors. Third drop?

b.student_note: Drops subtract from the rise — walk the loop with signs.

c.student_note: 12 − 9 = 3. Finish the loop.

questions.text: Convert 0.02 A to mA.

b.student_note: Milli is smaller, so the number grows: ×1000.

c.student_note: Three zeros: ×1000 exactly.

questions.text: A heater (100 Ω) runs on 200 V for 5 s. Heat produced?

b.student_note: 400 W is the rate; ×5 s gives energy.

c.student_note: Power here is V²/R, not V·R.

questions.text: V = 9 V, R = 3 Ω. Current?

b.student_note: Current divides V by R.

c.student_note: Ohm's law divides here.

questions.text: An ideal wire connects two points in a circuit. Voltage between them?

b.student_note: 'Ideal' wire means no drop: 0 V.

c.student_note: No splitting here — zero resistance, zero drop.

questions.text: Cartesian convention: object is 20 cm in front of a mirror. Object distance u?

b.student_note: In front of the mirror is the negative side here.

c.student_note: Zero is the pole, not the object.

d.student_note: No doubling — just attach the sign: −20 cm.

questions.text: Concave mirror, f = −10 cm, object at u = −30 cm. Image distance v?

b.student_note: Carry every minus through the algebra.

c.student_note: Concave f is negative here — the sign picks the formula's behaviour.

questions.text: A convex lens forms an image. A student uses the mirror formula with R signs. This is?
solution_steps: Lenses and mirrors have different sign maps.
Use the lens formula for lenses.

b.student_note: Mirror rules don't transfer to lenses — pick by device.

c.student_note: The formula choice itself is the gap, not just signs.

d.student_note: Units are fine — the formula choice is the point.

questions.text: m = −2 for a mirror image. The image is?

b.student_note: Minus means inverted (real) here; plus means erect.

c.student_note: Negative and erect never pair — recheck the sign map.

questions.text: Light goes air (n=1) → glass (n=1.5) at 30° to the normal. sin(r)?

b.student_note: Denser medium bends toward normal — sin r is smaller: divide.

c.student_note: The n = 1.5 still divides.

d.student_note: 1.5 is the index, not the sine.

questions.text: When can total internal reflection occur?

options.text: Denser to rarer, beyond critical angle

b.student_note: TIR only goes denser → rarer.

c.student_note: Small angles still refract — past critical is the trigger.

d.student_note: Two conditions gate TIR — media order plus angle.

questions.text: Convex mirror, f = +15 cm, object at u = −20 cm (Cartesian signs). Image distance v?

b.student_note: Behind-mirror images are positive here.

d.student_note: Two slips in one — sign and reciprocal. One line at a time.

questions.text: Light enters water (denser). It bends?

b.student_note: Denser means toward normal.

c.student_note: It still enters — bent, not bounced.

questions.text: A real image forms 30 cm in front of a mirror. v?

b.student_note: Real = in front = negative side here.

c.student_note: No doubling — just the sign: −30 cm.

questions.text: A lens question asks for image distance, but an option gives m = +0.5. Picking it means?

options.text: Compute v — m is not a distance

b.student_note: m has no length units — reread what is asked.

c.student_note: Magnification is unitless.

questions.text: A virtual image forms behind the mirror. Its v sign?

b.student_note: Behind the mirror is positive here.

c.student_note: Behind means a nonzero distance.

d.student_note: Every distance carries a sign here.

questions.text: f = −20 cm, u = −20 cm (concave). v?

c.student_note: Compute 1/v, don't echo.

questions.text: Glass → air, incidence 50°, critical 42°. What happens?

b.student_note: 50° > 42° flips it to TIR.

c.student_note: Glass is transparent here — it reflects.

questions.text: n1 = 1, n2 = 1.33, incidence 45° (sin = 0.707). sin(r)?

b.student_note: Divide by the denser index: 0.707/1.33.

c.student_note: The 1.33 still divides.

d.student_note: 1.33 is the index, not the sine.

questions.text: A curved-shiny-spoon back (convex) vs front (concave). Image in the back is?
solution_steps: Pick the lens/mirror behaviour by shape.

b.student_note: Back of spoon is convex — virtual and diminished.

c.student_note: Real images invert.

b.student_note: Keep signs through the fractions.

c.student_note: Compute 1/v.

questions.text: Gas temperature rises from 27°C to 327°C. By what factor does absolute temperature grow?

b.student_note: Gas laws need Kelvin — convert first, then ratio.

c.student_note: 300 K is the start, not the factor.

questions.text: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on the piston. ΔU? (Physics sign: W by system)

b.student_note: Work done BY the gas leaves the system — subtract it.

c.student_note: Heat in is +, work out is −: 500 − 200.

questions.text: An insulated gas expands quickly with no heat exchange. Temperature?
solution_steps: Work drains internal energy, so it cools.

b.explanation: Missed adiabatic Q = 0 and flipped the effect.
b.student_note: 'Insulated, no heat exchange' sets Q = 0 — expansion then cools the gas.

c.student_note: Constant temperature needs heat flow; insulated blocks it.

questions.text: An ideal gas expands isothermally. ΔU?
solution_steps: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on T: ΔU = 0.

b.explanation: Missed that isothermal fixes U for ideal gas.
b.student_note: 'Isothermal' pins temperature, and U follows temperature.

c.explanation: Assumed expansion drains U at constant T.
c.student_note: Heat flows in to compensate — ΔU stays 0.

d.student_note: Here Q becomes work, not internal energy.

questions.text: 300 J of work is done ON a gas and 100 J of heat leaves it. ΔU?
solution_steps: W on system is +300; heat leaving is −100.

b.student_note: Leaving heat is negative: 300 − 100.

c.student_note: Work done ON the gas adds energy: +300.

d.student_note: Fix one sign at a time: W on = +, Q out = −.

questions.text: Which statement separates heat from temperature?
solution_steps: Temperature is a state; heat is transfer.

options.text: Heat is stored in hot bodies

b.student_note: Bodies store internal energy; heat is energy in transit.

c.student_note: Temperature doesn't flow — heat does.

questions.text: Gas is compressed quickly (adiabatic). Sign of W (physics: W by system) and ΔU?
solution_steps: Compression: work is done ON gas, so W is negative.

b.student_note: Compression is work ON the gas: W negative, U rises.

c.student_note: Quick insulated squeeze heats the gas.

questions.text: Convert 37°C to Kelvin.

b.student_note: Add 273 for Kelvin.

c.student_note: Kelvin is larger: add.

questions.text: A gas expands slowly at constant temperature, doing 150 J of work. Heat absorbed?
solution_steps: Isothermal ideal gas: ΔU = 0, so Q = W.

b.student_note: No temperature change still moves energy: Q = W = 150 J in.

c.student_note: Energy must enter to fund the work.

questions.text: 1 cal ≈ 4.2 J. A snack bar releases 100 cal of heat. In joules?

b.student_note: Multiply by 4.2 for joules.

c.student_note: 4.2 converts one cal; scale to 100.

d.student_note: Joules are bigger numbers here: multiply.

questions.text: Convert 0°C to Kelvin.

b.student_note: 0°C is 273 K.

c.student_note: Kelvin adds: 0 + 273.

questions.text: Q = +200 J into gas, W = +50 J done BY gas. ΔU?

b.student_note: Work BY the gas subtracts.

c.student_note: Heat in is positive.

questions.text: A thermos (insulated) is shaken. Heat exchange Q?

b.student_note: 'Insulated' sets Q = 0 — shaking adds work, not heat.

c.student_note: A thermos blocks heat flow.

questions.text: Isothermal compression does −80 J of work (W by system). Heat flow?

b.student_note: Compression pushes energy in as work; heat must leave.

c.student_note: Isothermal still exchanges heat.

questions.text: Two bodies at the same temperature are touched. Net heat flow?

b.student_note: Same temperature means no drive.

c.student_note: Flow needs a difference first.

d.student_note: Size sets capacity, not direction here.

questions.text: Q = +100 J, W = 0 (rigid box). ΔU?

b.student_note: W = 0, so all 100 J stays as ΔU.

c.student_note: Heat in is positive.

questions.text: A 2 kg block slides down a rough ramp, dropping 5 m; friction does −40 J of work (g = 10). Speed at bottom?

b.student_note: Friction work counts: 100 − 40 = 60 J becomes motion.

c.student_note: Account friction inside the energy balance, not after.

questions.text: An insulated gas expands adiabatically, doing 120 J of work on the piston. ΔU?

b.explanation: Took work done by gas as positive ΔU.
b.student_note: Work leaving as expansion drains U: −120 J.

c.student_note: Adiabatic pins Q, not ΔU — work still moves energy.

d.student_note: ΔU equals the work here: 120 J.
